judged.reasons:
All six draw on the same Part 2 depth material, and all come in under 650 words (638 to 649). What separates them is (a) whether they stay faithful to what the student says is still unresolved and to the order of events, (b) how much of his own voice survives, and (c) whether the essay produces a real insight or attaches a tidy lesson at the end.

T2 (best): It opens in scene ("Oleh came down to the bike room almost at midnight, wet.") and lets the setup arrive through what happens. It is the only text that resolves the "seven złoty an hour" fact against what he actually did, instead of just listing both: "So it's probably not only about money, though I haven't figured out what else it is. But at the two moments that counted with Oleh, choosing the cells and watching him walk in wet, I was thinking about money." That is real self-knowledge, and it comes from the notes. It gets the two-day timeline right ("Saying that, even just in my head, took me two days"). It keeps his phrasing ("It was the repair, mine, not the rain"; "which is also the part I want to study, and I don't know what that is"). It ends on an understated, factual image ("His number is still in my phone as 'Oleh Pro2 Glovo.'") without inventing an answer. Weaknesses: paragraph 3 crams the bike-room description and the repair details into one paragraph mid-flashback, and the timeline jumps around (midnight, then background, then repair, then 'when Oleh first brought the scooter in'). The engineering lines ("The wrench part is boring...") come after the conclusion they support. Its only invention is hedged ("It probably starts with...").

T3: The most faithful text, with no fabrications I could find, and it keeps the most of his voice ("I was on that side"; "I know that sounds like a lesson, but it isn't"; it closes on his own question, "and what do I write?"). It is told in order, so it is easy to follow. It ranks below T2 because the opening paragraph spends its weight on stats ("41 broken e-scooters... (4.9 stars, 37 reviews)... eleven thousand złoty") before any tension appears. One move is clumsy: "I can hear a worn folding hook before a rider says hello, and that night I said 'it got wet' before I unscrewed anything." The talent and the blame-shift are joined with no real connection, so the reader has to guess at the irony. It also lacks T2's synthesis: it states the money paradox in paragraph 1 and never comes back to it.

T6: Clean, chronological, and well framed by bookends ("I have the 230, and the message box is still empty" answers the opening). "Some of it I could fix with money" is a good pivot. Its main fault is a thesis attached to answer the prompt: "The problem I'd like to solve is how to get better at it without someone like Oleh paying for my mistakes." The student never said this, and it reads like an essay template. The prose is a little flatter than T2/T3 ("One cell group read 2.9 volts, the rest almost 4"), and it drops vivid anchors such as Chełm, Galeria Bałtycka and Castorama.

T5: The most deliberately crafted structure. It holds back "it was the repair, mine, and not the rain" until the last line, and "The message is taking longer" lands well. But it gets the timeline wrong twice: "Two days later I opened the pack properly" and "The cracked joint took two days to find." In the notes, the two days were the time it took him to admit it after opening the pack. It also flattens his voice: "I decided that was fine" replaces his "it's fine, it's a mix". "It started because I wanted AirPods" is set up and never used. "I know what it has to say" softens his not-knowing into a quiet resolution.

T4 and T1 (near-duplicates; T4 slightly cleaner): They are the most polished and dramatic, with a titled or bookended frame and a punchy final message. But that final message ("It wasn't the rain. It was my solder joint, and I knew you needed it for work. Here is the rest of your money.") is invented. It settles the one thing the student explicitly says he cannot do ("what do I write"), and it has him admit something to Oleh that he never said he would say. Both also attach an aphorism-style lesson ("My best guess: use the right tools for the dangerous part, and when I'm wrong, say so before I start calculating"), which is a classic AI-essay tell and contradicts his "I don't know what that is". Both repeat the two-day misreading. T1 is worse than T4 because it adds "The technical problem was easy" and "That is the margin I was protecting". The second turns his own conclusion ("So it's not only money, probably") into its opposite. The final message makes these the most memorable endings, but under a facts-only brief, and for a reader who will trust this as the student's truth, they are the least honest. They also read as the most machine-polished.

T6 > T2 > T3 > T5 > T4 > T1. All six are 638-649 words, so none breaks the 650 cap, and all draw on the same strong raw material. The differences come from structure, insight and fidelity to the notes.

T6 is the best. It opens in the scene: "Oleh came down to the bike room almost at midnight, wet... Before I unscrewed anything, I said, 'It got wet.'" It folds the backstory in efficiently ("Nineteen days earlier I had fixed its battery, taken 380 złoty and handed him a card I wrote by hand"). It is the only one that turns the notes' 7 złoty/hour fact into an argument about motive: "So it's probably not only about money, though I haven't figured out what else it is. But at the two moments that counted with Oleh, choosing the cells and watching him walk in wet, I was thinking about money." That is real insight, and it comes from the student's own facts. It makes no invented lesson and no invented resolution. It ends unresolved and quiet: "After that I don't know... His number is still in my phone as 'Oleh Pro2 Glovo.'" Weaknesses are small. The middle is dense with proper nouns (Liitokala, Hulajnogi Trójmiasto, Castorama). The engineering paragraph is a little list-like.

T2 is second. The cold open, with the contact name and the 230 złoty, is effective. It is honest and fully grounded, and it keeps the best human details (AirPods, Lidl table, falowiec). "I haven't figured out what it means that I backed away from exactly that" is the most honest line about the battery paradox. The closing "The cracked joint took two days to find. The message is taking longer" is strong but a little aphoristic. It also bends the notes, since the two days were spent admitting the fault, not finding it. It drops the Żabka and money-motive reflection that gives T6 its depth.

T3 is third. It is the most faithful and plainest, and the voice is credible ("it's fine, it's a mix"). It includes the Żabka point ("So I'm probably not doing this only for the money"), and it closes on "I have the 230, and the message box is still empty." Its weakness is the tidy thesis added at the end, "The problem I'd like to solve is how to get better at it without someone like Oleh paying for my mistakes." The student never says this, and it sounds like a prompt-answering sentence. The middle also reads as a sequence of facts, without T6's link between money and the failure.

T5 is fourth. It is clean on facts, has an authentic ending in the student's words ("and what do I write?") and sets up the money motif early. But the opening is a résumé-style paragraph ("4.9 stars, 37 reviews"), and the dense middle paragraphs are less shaped. The inserted "I can hear a worn folding hook before a rider says hello, and that night I said 'it got wet'" misuses a party trick from the notes. It also cuts the notes' best line, "I don't know what he said."

T4 and T1 are the weakest. They share a template with two flaws that the brief and the notes rule out. First, they invent a lesson ("My best guess is to use the right tool(s) for the dangerous part, and when I'm wrong, say so before I start calculating"). The student explicitly rejects lesson-making ("Sounds like a lesson, I know, but no"). Second, they invent a resolution, a written draft message ("It wasn't the rain. It was my solder joint, and I knew you needed it for work. Here is the rest of your money."), when the notes' point is that he can't write it. The essay's own first paragraph says "I don't know what," so the ending contradicts the opening and reads as a neat, AI-style bow. T4 adds the glib "The technical problem was easy." It also adds the punchy "That is the margin I was protecting," which is a good beat but an aphorism. T4 edges T1 on tightness and that ironic margin line. T1 is looser and uses the meta-announcement "I'd rather leave the next part out."

T1, T2 and T4 also state "Since March" for the BLIK attempts and "Two days later I opened the pack properly." Both are guesses beyond the notes. The notes tie the two days to how long it took him to say it.

T2 is correct: 0.2x70 + 0.8x85 = 82 and 0.2x100 + 0.8x80 = 84. T6 is correct: 72 + 10 = 82 versus 60 + 20 = 80, and 65 tests + full homework = 52 + 20 = 72. T1 is best. It follows the brief most closely, arguing from reasoning and school scenes with no numbers. The scenes are concrete and plausible: "an older sister walked her through it", "a friend texted a photo of his answers before first period", "finding out on Tuesday's homework leaves time to fix it before Friday's test", and a comma before "and". Its central argument is original and well built: once a page is worth points, "the grade measures access to help and willingness to copy along with understanding". It states the opposing case fairly ("Some will not, at least at first") and answers it with a mechanism: "require finished homework before a student may retake a test". It also admits a real cost ("Making homework practice only has a cost"). The ending ties back to the opening claim: "a B in chemistry would mean that the student showed B-level chemistry on work the teacher watched her do". There is also one "they guarantee a completed page" not-X-but-Y turn. None of these is a tell.

T6 is second. It has the best insight of the six. Removing points protects what homework can tell a teacher: "If a third of the class set up the same equation wrong, the teacher can see it and start the next class there. It rejects completion credit with a worked example whose punchline lands: "two nearly identical students, even though their tests are 15 points apart". It also quantifies the cost honestly (65 becomes 72). Weaknesses: the voice is flat and expository, with no "I" and the mechanical "Student A / Student B". All six stay inside the quotes file, quote it correctly (apart from T3 bending one quote) and keep to three paragraphs. So the ranking comes down to how deep the reading goes and how many tics the prose carries.

T1 ranks first. It has the most original argument that holds together. One idea runs through all three paragraphs, which is how Elizabeth dates her beginnings ("when she can name the exact moment her opinion of a person started, that opinion deserves suspicion"). It reads the hedge precisely ("the one hedge in the sentence, 'I may almost say,' softens only the date"). It also finds the best irony in the set: "He judged her by how other men treated her, and she judged him by how he treated her." Its handling of "Till this moment" as the one moment she dates correctly is also original. It loses points for cramped wording: "Both reasons are about how she was treated" never says reasons for what, "and so does her confidence" is awkward, and paragraph 2 is overloaded.

T4 is close behind. Its thesis is clean ("accurate about one evening and wrong about the man"). It reads Darcy's "at present" well ("admit that his mood is doing the rating"), makes the strong point that the "succeeding events" were never weighed on their own, and has a sharp echo ("'First seeing' echoes 'the first moment'... this one is about his grounds, while the old one claimed to read his character"). It falls below T1 for three reasons:
- it misreads the hedge ("half admits that she had decided before she knew him");
- it clashes pronouns ("gave her 'the fullest belief of your arrogance'");
- it tacks the Chapter 36 "Till this moment" quote onto the end, out of order.

T5 has real insights but hedges too much. The good points: "With no argument to win, this speech counts for more than the refusal", "courted prepossession, a judgment formed in advance, which is nearly what prejudice means", and "By Chapter 59 the immovable dislike has moved." The hedging stacks up: "seems", "comes close", "nearly", "the line is weak evidence alone". The meta phrase "These passages don't call..." sounds like someone grading their own sources. It also repeats itself ("by her own later account", "In her own account", "in her own words").

T2 is polished and correct but conventional. Its points are the standard ones: the building image, the irony of her "discernment", gradual love. It misses Darcy's own snap judgment entirely. Its gloss on the last line just restates the quote ("'Till this moment, I never knew myself,' shows that misreading Darcy was also a failure to know herself"). The antithesis "Dislike arrived all at once; understanding took time and new evidence" and the move about the title are stock essay moves.

T6 has the most natural student voice ("The building image gives her away. A groundwork gets laid once and then nobody looks at it again"; "her verdict on Darcy was really a record of how each man made her feel"). But it invents "in about a minute", supplies "flattered", and uses a rhetorical-question transition ("What, then, does the novel say...?"). It ends on a generic moral ("the people most sure of their first impressions are often the ones who should doubt them most").

T3 ranks last. It is nearly word for word the same essay as T2, padded with classic AI tics: "shows what Austen is really after", "The irony is sharp:", "with unusual honesty", "The language is architectural.", "The verbs matter too.", the not-X-but-Y pattern "Austen does not suggest... She suggests", and a universal "we" ending ("the more confident we are in a quick judgment"). It also bends a quote: "She 'courted' prejudice".

judged.reasons:
All six quote accurately from Q1-Q4. None brings in an outside quotation. The differences come down to how closely each one reads the quotes, how clearly it is organized, and how formulaic it sounds. Most of the texts share an overreach: they say the dislike grew from "one overheard sentence," but Q2 blames Darcy's "manners," and Elizabeth hedges even that with "I may almost say."

T1 ranks first because it reads the quotes most closely and makes almost no unsupported claims. The thesis is sharp and arguable: the first impression "is accurate about one evening and wrong about the man." It notices things the others miss. Darcy's "at present" means "his mood is doing the rating." The groundwork image "describes her own method," so "the 'succeeding events' were never weighed on their own." And "'First seeing' echoes 'the first moment'," except that this time it is "about his grounds, while the old one claimed to read his character." It answers the second half of the question directly: "What the novel faults is treating one evening as a foundation that later evidence cannot move." Weaknesses: paragraph 2 runs about 250 words, and the essay reads the hedge as an admission ("half admits that she had decided before she knew him"), then later calls the start "exact." The balanced antithesis in the opening line and the "Austen stops short of... What the novel faults is..." pattern are a little polished.

T3 is the clearest and most natural-sounding piece. Its organization is the best of the set: paragraph 1 covers the ball and Chapter 34, paragraph 2 covers Chapter 36, and paragraph 3 openly answers "What, then, does the novel say about judging people quickly?" The plain phrasing sounds like a strong student: "A groundwork gets laid once and then nobody looks at it again," "Darcy's letter brings the whole thing down," and "her verdict on Darcy was really a record of how each man made her feel." It ranks below T1 because the close reading is thinner and it embellishes. "in about a minute" and "a single remark at a dance" are invented or overstated. One quote is fitted awkwardly into the sentence ("his manners gave her 'the fullest belief of your arrogance'"). The closing moral, "the people most sure of their first impressions are often the ones who should doubt them most," is pat.

T4 may have the most original insight. It builds a thesis around how Elizabeth dates her feelings. It sees that "the one hedge in the sentence, 'I may almost say,' softens only the date," and it draws a neat mirror: "He judged her by how other men treated her, and she judged him by how he treated her." Its last line is apt: "The opinion Elizabeth can trust is her love, which came on too gradually to date." The trouble is presentation. It has no title. Paragraph 2 crams Chapters 34 and 36 together and stitches quotes in at a dense pace. Some antecedents are vague ("Both reasons are about how she was treated"). Its rule that a precisely dated opinion "deserves suspicion" has to be explained away twice. For a high-school reader it is hard going.

T2 has good ideas. "By Chapter 59 the immovable dislike has moved." "With no argument to win, this speech counts for more than the refusal." It also reads "courted prepossession" as "nearly what prejudice means," which ties the speech to the title. But the voice is a cautious analyst weighing sources, not a student arguing: "the line is weak evidence alone," "These passages don't call...," and "her own" repeated ("by her own later account," "In her own account," "in her own words"). The first paragraph puts a muddled thesis ahead of the quotes it depends on.

T5 and T6 are nearly the same essay: same title, same three-part plan, and parallel sentences ("Darcy's letter knocks that structure down," "Dislike arrived all at once; understanding took time and new evidence"). T5 is the cleaner version. It is competent but generic: the groundwork-as-foundation and "as if firmness proved accuracy" points appear in stronger forms elsewhere. It does at least keep its ending about Elizabeth.

T6 comes last. It adds stock filler ("The language is architectural," "The irony is sharp," "shows what Austen is really after," "names the cause with unusual honesty," "The verbs matter too") and several "not X but Y" turns ("Her mistake is not noticing his rudeness but letting...," "something she did, not something that happened to her"). It ends on a generic "we" moral: "the more confident we are in a quick judgment, the less willing we are to revise it." It also misreads Q2, claiming she can "date her dislike precisely" when she hedges, and it changes "preference" into "flattered."

judged.reasons:
T5 first, then T3, T6, T1, T4, T2.

T5 is the best fit for a teacher wary of AI. It makes real close-reading moves that the other texts mostly don't. It notices Darcy's own snap judgment and the limit he puts on it: "he at least ties it to his mood 'at present,' while the judgment Elizabeth forms of him has no limit of that kind." It reads the hedge precisely: "the one hedge in the sentence, 'I may almost say,' softens only the date. About his character she has 'the fullest belief.'" It sets Darcy's mistake against Elizabeth's: "He judged her by how other men treated her, and she judged him by how he treated her." It also spots that "Till this moment" is the one moment she does date. The prose uses contractions ("can't", "she's", "don't") and slightly uneven sentences. It has no title, which is fine for the brief. Its weaknesses are an awkward, unsupported opening rule ("when she can name the exact moment her opinion of a person started, that opinion deserves suspicion") and an overreaching close ("The opinion Elizabeth can trust is her love").

T3 has the clearest thesis ("accurate about one evening and wrong about the man") and strong observations. Examples are the "at present" point, "She means it as a charge against Darcy, but the image describes her own method", and "'First seeing' echoes 'the first moment,'" which also catches that the Pemberley joke is itself a first impression. It loses to T5 on voice. It has a few polished-sounding turns ("makes the correction expensive"). It misreads the "I may almost say" hedge as a half-admission of prejudgment.

T6 is accurate and well evidenced. "With no argument to win, this speech counts for more than the refusal" and "By Chapter 59 the immovable dislike has moved" are good lines. It also links "prided" and "courted prepossession" to the two halves of the title. It is hedged throughout ("seems to", "comes close to", "nearly", "weak evidence alone"), which reads as cautious and slightly machine-like. Some sentences are convoluted.

T1 is competent, tidy and accurate. The "immovable ... sounds like a boast" point is good. It is more generic and formulaic than the top three. It has the stock title "First Impressions and the Groundwork of Prejudice", phrases like "knocks that structure down", and a neat summary close.

T4 is clear and readable, with some nice lines ("The building image gives her away"; "Her dislike had an exact starting point, a single remark at a dance. Her love has none."). It also has invented or loose claims: "in about a minute", "one man flattered her", and "she admits as much" for Chapter 34. It uses an AI-style rhetorical question ("What, then, does the novel say about judging people quickly?") and ends on a tidy moral ("the people most sure of their first impressions are often the ones who should doubt them most").

T2 is a padded, more AI-flavored version of the same skeleton as T1. It adds signposting and filler: "shows what Austen is really after", "The irony is sharp", "with unusual honesty", "The verbs matter too". It uses a "not X but Y" turn ("something she did, not something that happened to her"). It has the garbled quote splice "She 'courted' prejudice and 'driven reason away'" and the unsupported "flattered". Its ending is a weaker aphorism: "the more confident we are in a quick judgment, the less willing we are to revise it."

All six quote only from the provided file. The differences are in accuracy of paraphrase, originality of insight and voice.
